chapterTitle: Insurance: Don't Sweat the Small Stuff

facts.claim: Employer-plan research found expected savings above 500 dollars per year from high-deductible options across a wide spending range.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because premium savings and employer account contributions exceeded the extra deductible exposure in the compared designs.
facts.commonError: A lower deductible always produces lower total financial risk.
facts.whyWrong: Higher premiums can outweigh the reduced out-of-pocket payment in every spending state.

facts.claim: Prescription use fell more when drugs were subject to the consumer-directed plan deductible.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the upfront price made patients reduce utilization rather than selectively preserve every high-value medicine.
facts.commonError: Patients reliably distinguish essential from unnecessary care when cost sharing rises.
facts.whyWrong: Use declined for chronic-disease medicines as well as lower-value consumption.

facts.claim: Pitney Bowes lowered copayments for asthma, hypertension, and diabetes medicines.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because reducing the price of high-value drugs increased adherence and could avoid more expensive complications.
facts.commonError: Value-based insurance applies the same deductible to every service.
facts.whyWrong: It varies cost sharing with clinical value.

facts.claim: Insurance is most valuable for a low-probability loss large enough to threaten financial stability.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because risk pooling converts a potentially ruinous shock into a predictable premium.
facts.commonError: Insurance should cover every small repair because claims feel like getting value back.
facts.whyWrong: Administrative cost and insurer margin make routine small-loss coverage expensive.

facts.claim: A plan dominates another when it is no worse in every relevant spending state and better in at least one.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because no possible outcome gives the dominated plan a financial advantage.
facts.commonError: A dominated plan may still be optimal simply because its deductible is lower.
facts.whyWrong: The premium difference can more than offset deductible savings everywhere.

facts.claim: Deductible aversion is the tendency to pay too much premium to avoid out-of-pocket exposure.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a salient possible payment receives more weight than the certain annual premium difference.
facts.commonError: Selecting a low deductible always reflects greater objective risk protection.
facts.whyWrong: Some low-deductible plans raise cost even in the worst spending case.

facts.claim: An extended warranty typically insures a manageable product loss while embedding seller cost and profit.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because expected claims are smaller than the warranty price after administration and margin.
facts.commonError: A warranty is a bargain whenever replacement would be annoying.
facts.whyWrong: Annoyance does not make the expected payout exceed the premium.

facts.claim: Behavioral hazard occurs when cost sharing causes people to skip valuable care rather than only wasteful care.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because limited information, present bias, and liquidity constraints make patients respond to price without perfect value sorting.
facts.commonError: Higher out-of-pocket prices reduce only medically unnecessary use.
facts.whyWrong: Evidence shows essential medications can be reduced too.

facts.claim: An On My Own HSA earmarks premium savings for deductible expenses.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a visible health account makes self-insurance resources feel protected from ordinary spending.
facts.commonError: Choosing a high deductible requires leaving the possible deductible entirely unfunded.
facts.whyWrong: Premium savings and employer contributions can be reserved in the HSA.

allowedAnchors.label: deductible design
allowedAnchors.text: A deductible sets how much loss the insured pays before coverage begins, trading lower premiums against greater out-of-pocket exposure. Choosing the wrong deductible can guarantee higher expected cost, while poorly targeted cost sharing can suppress essential care.

allowedAnchors.label: Saurabh Bhargava, George Loewenstein, and Justin Sydnor / employer health-plan choices
allowedAnchors.text: Researchers compared employees' plan selections across firms offering low- and high-deductible options. Many selected financially dominated low-deductible plans, while the high-deductible option produced expected savings above 500 dollars a year across a broad range of spending. Deductible aversion can survive even when one plan is no better in any spending state.
hardSpecifics: expected savings above 500 dollars per year
employees chose financially dominated low-deductible plans

allowedAnchors.label: Peter Huckfeldt and colleagues / pharmaceutical deductibles
allowedAnchors.text: Two large firms switched employees to consumer-directed health plans, but only one subjected prescriptions to the deductible. Drug use fell most where prescriptions faced the deductible, including medicines for chronic disease. Patients do not reliably cut only low-value care when exposed to broad cost sharing.
hardSpecifics: two large employers switched to consumer-directed plans
prescriptions faced the deductible at one firm but were exempt at the other

allowedAnchors.label: Pitney Bowes / value-based insurance design
allowedAnchors.text: Pitney Bowes reduced copayments for medicines treating asthma, hypertension, and diabetes. Adherence increased, and higher drug spending was offset by lower condition-related medical spending. Cost sharing should be lower for care with high clinical value.

higher adherence accompanied lower condition-related medical costs
